chapter_theme: The marks of the soul (பசு இலக்கணம்), given through the swan (அன்னம்): the Lord is known within as an unfading lamp, and soul and Lord are two swans that never part; the swan that holds itself a separate one does not reach its gain.
structure_note: The title is about the soul, but the two verses speak of the swan; the swan (hamsa) as an image of the soul is the link.

2005.reading: The One who is perceived as far as one contemplates him, the Supreme whom the recited Vedas study, the unfading lamp within me: I came to know him as of the nature of the swan.
2005.nuance: அன்ன மயம் may be 'of the swan' (hamsa, the soul and the breath in yogic usage) or 'made of food' (annamaya, the body's sheath). The next verse's swans favour the first; the second would mean he is known in the body.

2006.reading: There are two swans on the river bank; the two keep close and never leave each other; if a swan holds that its state is a single one apart, that deluded, separated swan will not reach the gain.
2006.nuance: The two swans are commonly taken as the soul and the Lord, like the two birds on one tree of the Upanishads; they may also be read as the two breaths. பின்ன மட அன்னம் is the swan that is foolishly divided off, or that thinks itself apart.

links.note: 2006 has the two swans that never part and faults the swan that holds itself apart; 2017 says there is no difference of soul and Siva once Siva is known. Both deny the soul a separate standing.
